context.why:
US-1 landed the component and the Plans page: the provider's element is emitted with the pricing table identifier and the publishable key, and the page reads both from the project's settings. This story adds the one attribute that decides whether a purchase can be attributed to anybody.

The installed backend matches a customer at the provider back to an application user by EMAIL ADDRESS ALONE. Confirmed in its source at drf_stripe/stripe_api/customers.py:116-117: django_user_query_filters = {DJANGO_USER_EMAIL_FIELD: customer.email}. There is no other identifier in that path, and the attribute the provider built for exactly this reconciliation, client-reference-id, is read nowhere in the whole installed package.

So a signed-in person who clicks a plan, lands on the provider's checkout and types a different address gets one of two outcomes: the backend raises when the purchase arrives and the subscription attaches to nobody, or a second application user is created around the address they typed and the person who paid still sees nothing on their own subscription page. Passing the account's address closes that, costs one attribute, and is what the provider documents the attribute for.

The component already declares customer_email and does not read it. This story wires it: an address supplied as an attribute wins; otherwise the signed-in person's, read from request.user in the context the way portal_link.html already reads csrf_token; where there is neither, the attribute is OMITTED ENTIRELY rather than emitted empty, because an empty customer-email is not the same instruction to the provider as an absent one.

spec_sections: User Story 2 - A purchase belongs to the person who made it
prior_decisions: The address is passed because the backend reads no other identifier. Do not add client-reference-id: passing a value nothing consumes would look like a guarantee and provide none.
An attribute supplied by a template author wins over the signed-in person's address, because a project placing the component on a page of its own may have a better answer than the session does.
The component reads no settings. Reading request.user out of the template context is not a settings read and is the established shape here — portal_link.html reads csrf_token the same way.
The component imposes no sign-in requirement of its own (FR-009). It must render for an anonymous visitor with no address and no error.
WATCH — assert the attribute's ABSENCE as absence, not as emptiness. A test that accepts customer-email="" does not hold FR-005.
WATCH — a signed-in person whose account carries no email address is a real case: Django's user model allows a blank email. Scenario 2 is about that person.

D3 — tests/test_urls.py's routing registry was updated by Forge after US-1, as the mechanical consequence of routing the Plans page through its own view. It is now a pre-existing test again; do not touch it.

acceptance.given_when_then: Given the component rendered for a signed-in person holding an email address, when the output is read, then the element carries customer-email with that address; given a signed-in person with no address, then no customer-email attribute appears at all and the rest of the element is unchanged; given an anonymous visitor, then none appears; given customer_email supplied as an attribute, then that value is used in preference to the signed-in person's.

Given a signed-in person opening the Plans page, when it renders, then the provider's element on that page carries that person's own address — asserted end to end through the page, not through the component alone.

Given the component, when it renders, then customer_email wins where supplied, the signed-in person's address is used where it is not, and the attribute is omitted entirely where there is neither; and the header comment says why the address is passed at all.
Given docs/plans-page.md, when someone reads it, then it says where the address comes from, that an attribute wins, and what its absence means for a purchase.
